name: Real-time / dynamic pricing inputs
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Real-time / dynamic pricing inputs (per-SKU / per-zone / per-time demand counters, sell-through-rate over rolling windows, view-to-cart velocities, basket-affinity recency, surge-pricing supply/demand ratios, competitor-scrape-driven price-anchor features, demand-response load signals) — i.e., the live feature backend that feeds a downstream pricing rules engine or pricing ML model (XGBoost / contextual bandits / reinforcement-learning / elasticity estimators / continuous-pricing scorers) for retail, e-comm, hotels, airlines, ride-hailing, food-delivery, marketplaces, energy, and ticketing buyers.
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A pricing engine (retail RGM, e-comm dynamic-pricing service, hotel/airline revenue-management system, ride-hailing surge engine, marketplace fee/repricer, energy real-time-pricing optimizer, or ticketing repricer) decides, on every view / search / add-to-cart / availability lookup / quote request / ride request / hourly tick — typically within tens of milliseconds — what price (or price multiplier) to display, based on per-SKU / per-zone / per-(SKU, zone, hour) / per-(origin, destination, day) rolling demand velocities, sell-through rates, view-to-cart conversion windows, basket-affinity recency, competitor price anchors, and supply/demand ratios.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Compute real-time demand counters per (SKU, zone, hour-of-day) — views, clicks, add-to-carts, checkouts, cart-abandons, search-impressions — over rolling 1m / 5m / 15m / 1h / 24h / 7d windows so an XGBoost or elasticity model can score a price candidate within the page-render budget. 2) Compute rolling sell-through-rate per SKU / category / store as count(unit_sold, W) / inventory_received_or_starting_stock, with the documented retailer thresholds (below 20 % triggers markdown, below 10 % triggers transfer, above 80 % triggers reorder) — directly turn the metric into an action signal. 3) Compute view-to-cart velocity and view-to-cart conversion rate per (SKU, traffic-source, geo) on sliding windows to detect demand-surge SKUs (the e-comm analogue of Uber's surge signal) and feed contextual bandits. 4) Maintain per-(geohash | H3 cell | zone) supply/demand ratio counters for ride-hailing surge (Uber, Lyft Prime Time, DoorDash Peak Pay, Instacart Busy Pay) and food-delivery fee surge, updated every 30-60 s. 5) Maintain per-(origin, destination, departure-date, fare-class | room-type, check-in-date) booking-velocity, search-velocity, look-to-book ratio, and 'distance from competitor price anchor' features for airline RM (PROS Real-Time Dynamic Pricing, Fetcherr) and hotel revenue management (PriceLabs, Beyond Pricing, IDeaS). 6) Maintain per-(event_id, seat-section) sales-velocity and time-to-sellout features for ticketing repricers (Ticketmaster Pricemaster / Platinum, StubHub). 7) Track competitor-price-anchor features (latest scraped competitor price, age of scrape, count of times competitor moved in last 24h, percentile rank vs catalog) per SKU/GTIN from Wiser / Sniffie-Pricen / Competera / Pricer24 / Skuuudle scrape feeds. 8) Maintain basket-affinity recency / co-purchase counters per (anchor_sku, candidate_sku) pair over 7d/30d for bundle-pricing and cross-sell discount decisions. 9) Maintain per-grid-cell / per-tariff energy load and demand-response signals for real-time-pricing utilities (ComEd Hourly Pricing, NYISO, demand-response programs).
domain_fit.event_shapes: Typical events landing in beava as @bv.event. E-commerce: view {ts, sku, user_id, session_id, geo_h3, traffic_source, device}, search {ts, query_hash, user_id, geo_h3}, add_to_cart {ts, sku, qty, list_price, session_id}, cart_abandon {ts, session_id, sku[], gmv_lost}, checkout / order {ts, sku[], qty[], unit_price[], total, user_id, geo_h3, payment_method}, inventory_update {ts, sku, store_id, on_hand_qty, received_qty}, price_change {ts, sku, store_id, old_price, new_price, source (own|competitor|promo)}, competitor_scrape_observation {ts, sku|gtin, competitor_id, observed_price, observed_availability, scrape_age_seconds, channel}, promo_redemption {ts, sku, promo_id, discount_pct}. Ride-hailing/food-delivery: ride_request {ts, rider_id, pickup_h3, dropoff_h3, vehicle_type}, driver_position {ts, driver_id, h3, status (online|busy|offline)}, ride_complete {ts, ride_id, fare, surge_multiplier}, restaurant_order {ts, restaurant_id, h3, etd}, courier_position {ts, courier_id, h3, status}. Travel: search {ts, origin, destination, dep_date, ret_date, pax, cabin, user_segment}, look_to_book pair (look event, book event), availability_query {ts, hotel_id, check_in, los, room_type}, booking {ts, hotel_id|flight_id, value, fare_class, advance_purchase_days}. Ticketing: event_search {ts, event_id, section}, ticket_view, ticket_purchase {ts, event_id, section, qty, price, seat_ids[]}. Energy: meter_read {ts, meter_id, kwh, grid_cell}, grid_dispatch_signal {ts, region, lmp_price}, dr_event {ts, region, target_curtailment_mw}. Volume is dominated by view / search / driver_position / meter_read events; high-fan-in dimensions are sku, geohash/H3, (origin,dest,date), (hotel_id,check_in), (event_id,section).
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of beava counters + velocity + n_unique + distance + distribution primitives over tumbling and sliding windows. Per-SKU: count(view, 1m/5m/15m/1h/24h), velocity(view), count(add_to_cart, 1h/24h), atc_conversion = count(add_to_cart, 1h) / count(view, 1h) (the canonical view-to-cart-rate), count(purchase, 1h/24h/7d), sell_through_rate_W = count(unit_sold, W) / received_qty_W, count(cart_abandon, 1h), velocity(price_change_own, 24h) (frequency rate-limit governor), n_unique(user_id, 1h) (distinct demand vs bot floor), distribution(observed_competitor_price, 7d) (T-Digest for percentile rank vs competitor set), distance(own_price - median_competitor_price, current) — the literal 'price-anchor distance' feature, distance(observed_price_competitor - last_observed, current) (competitor-move-detection), age_seconds(latest_competitor_scrape) (freshness governor). Per-(SKU, geohash | store_id | zone): per-store sell-through, per-store local demand-velocity. Per-(H3 cell, time-window) for ride-hailing: count(ride_request, 1m / 5m), count(driver_online, current), supply_demand_ratio = count(ride_request, 5m) / count(driver_available, current), velocity(ride_request) over 5-min sliding, distance(neighboring-cell supply, current) for spillover smoothing. Per-(origin, destination, dep_date) for airline: count(search, 1h/24h), count(book, 1h/24h/7d), look_to_book_ratio = book / search over W, velocity(book, 24h), days_to_departure, sum(remaining_capacity), distance(competitor_lowest_fare - own_fare). Per-(hotel_id, check_in_date) for hotel: count(search, 24h), count(book, 24h), pickup (book in last 24h vs prior baseline), occupancy_pct = booked / inventory, comp-set price anchor. Per-(event_id, section) for ticketing: count(view, 1h), count(purchase, 1h/24h), velocity(purchase) (sales velocity), seats_remaining, time_to_event, percentile(price vs secondary-market distribution). Per-(anchor_sku, candidate_sku) pair for basket-affinity: count(co_view, 24h/7d), count(co_purchase, 7d/30d), recency_seconds(last_co_purchase). Per-(grid_cell | tariff_id) for energy: rolling_load_kwh_5m, peak_to_average_ratio, count(dr_event_optin, 24h).
domain_fit.entity_grain: Primary keys span sku / gtin / variant_id (retail, e-comm, marketplace), (sku, store_id), (sku, geohash | H3 cell), h3_cell or geohash (ride-hailing, food-delivery surge), (h3_cell, time_bucket), (origin_iata, destination_iata, departure_date) and (origin_iata, destination_iata, departure_date, fare_class) (airline), (hotel_id, check_in_date) and (hotel_id, check_in_date, room_type) (hotel), (event_id, section) and (event_id, seat_id) (ticketing), (anchor_sku, candidate_sku) pair (basket affinity), (competitor_id, sku) and (competitor_id, gtin) (price anchors), (grid_cell, tariff_id) (energy), and tenant-scoped versions of all of the above for multi-merchant marketplace repricing.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate: 1m / 5m / 15m for surge and view-to-cart-velocity, 1h / 24h for sell-through and look-to-book, 7d / 30d for basket-affinity and seasonal demand baselines, 90d for elasticity / baseline-comparison. Tumbling 5-min or 15-min windows are standard for the surge / RGM pricing-cycle tick (PROS, Fetcherr, Uber surge — public descriptions cite 30-60 s update cadences for ride-hailing and 5-min for retail RM). Hopping windows for hourly retail price recalc. Approximate aggregates are widely acceptable: HLL for n_unique(user_id) per SKU (distinguishing organic demand from bot floors), CMS for top-K trending SKUs / top-K H3 cells, T-Digest for competitor-price percentile rank and for the price-distribution features used by Sniffie/Wiser/Competera. Exact aggregates are required for sell-through-rate (because retailers enforce action thresholds on the exact number) and for compliance-relevant pricing-frequency caps under EU price-anchoring rules (Omnibus Directive Art. 6a).
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once with idempotent counters keyed on event_id is sufficient for view/cart/click counters, surge ratios, and view-to-cart velocity (a duplicated view biases demand slightly upward, which is safe). Strict no-double-count is required only for (a) the inventory / sell-through ledger (the source-of-truth count of units shipped — most retailers source this from ERP, not from beava) and (b) audit-grade price-history under EU Omnibus and Digital Fairness Act personalised-pricing disclosure (transparency artifacts), which are warehouse-materialised, not in-memory.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Tens of milliseconds end-to-end, as stated by the buyer description. The published competitive bar is Tecton sub-10 ms p99 online feature read at 100k+ QPS and Hopsworks 7.5 ms p99 at 250k+ ops/sec; pricing decisions on a hot path (PDP render, surge fare quote, airline-shop, hotel-availability response) sit inside a 50-200 ms total page/quote budget of which the feature read should consume <20 ms. Repricing batch ticks (5-min hourly retail recalc, surge tick every 30-60 s) tolerate seconds. Beava's published sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get and ~684k EPS on a single M4 core comfortably outperform the published feature-store SLAs on the read side.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to single-digit seconds end-to-end for surge-style decisions (ride-hailing, food-delivery, flash-sale, ticketing-spike) and seconds-to-minutes for retail RGM. Tecton publicly cites 'feature freshness under one second' as the differentiator that wins dynamic-pricing buyers like DoorDash. Industry guidance for competitor-price anchor features is hourly to sub-hourly because scrape pipelines themselves are not sub-second. Beava's push-on-event model with no broker hop is materially fresher than the Kafka -> Flink -> Redis pipeline that Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Riskified, and most in-house pricing teams publish about. [uncertain]
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Highly buyer-dependent, generally write-heavy on the event ingest side. (a) E-commerce mid-size buyer (~10-50M monthly visitors): 5-50k EPS sustained on view + search + add-to-cart, bursts to 100-300k EPS during flash sales / Black Friday. (b) Ride-hailing / food-delivery single-region (Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart): driver-position events alone run tens to hundreds of thousands of EPS (one position update per driver per ~4-10 s × hundreds of thousands of active drivers per region). DoorDash publicly reports its Iguazu real-time event system at 'hundreds of billions of events per day' (~1-3M EPS aggregate across all use cases). Lyft uses Kafka for surge with Flink-keyed-by-H3-cell on 5-min sliding windows. (c) Airline single-carrier: 1-10k shop-requests/sec at peak; PROS / Fetcherr / Amadeus shop volumes are in that range. (d) Hotel revenue-management vendor (PriceLabs, Beyond, Duetto, IDeaS): low thousands EPS across many tenants. (e) Ticketing event drops: bursts of 10-100k EPS for 5-30 min during an on-sale. A single beava node at ~684k EPS comfortably covers single-region retail, hotel RM, airline RM, ticketing, and per-city ride-hailing surge; multi-city ride-hailing aggregate and global-scale e-comm flash sales exceed a single box. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Read-heavy 5:1 to 50:1 on the inline pricing path. Every view / search / availability query reads 20-100 features but typically writes only a handful (the same view event is at most one write). Surge / RGM repricing ticks are even more read-heavy because the tick reads aggregated state across many cells / SKUs and writes back only the resulting multipliers. Sell-through and price-anchor refresh paths are more balanced.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by SKU cardinality and composite-key (SKU, geo) / (SKU, competitor) state. A mid-sized retailer (~1-5M live SKUs, 1000 stores, 50 competitors tracked per SKU): ~1-5M SKUs × ~80 active counter slots × ~32 B ≈ 2.5-12 GB; ~5M × 1000 store-SKU pairs is unbounded without aggressive TTL on cold pairs (most SKUs sell at <10 stores in any window), realistic active is 50-200 M (SKU,store) pairs × 10 counters ≈ 15-60 GB; ~50 competitors × 5M SKU ≈ 250M competitor-anchor records × 5 counters ≈ 30-50 GB. Travel: ~10k city-pairs × ~365 dep_dates × ~20 fare_classes ≈ 70M rows × 20 counters ≈ 25 GB per airline. Hotel RM SaaS: ~1M listings × ~365 check-in_dates ≈ 365M × 10 counters ≈ 100 GB. Ride-hailing single city: ~5-20k H3 r9 cells × 10 counters ≈ trivial; global Uber-scale aggregate runs into the tens-of-millions of cells. Most single-buyer deployments fit on a 128-512 GB box; global-scale (Amazon retail, global Uber, global Booking.com) requires sharding. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly growing on SKU (catalog growth is bounded), explosive on (SKU, store_id) / (SKU, competitor_id) / (SKU, geohash) composite keys (long tail of inactive pairs), bounded on H3-cell per city (~5-20k r9 cells), explosive on (origin, dest, date, class) and (hotel_id, check_in_date) (capacity bounded by the booking horizon, typically 365 days × 20 classes), bounded on (event_id, section) for ticketing, bounded on grid_cell for energy. Top-K trending-SKU / top-K hot-H3-cell views are CMS / Top-K appropriate.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Short-fresh for surge / view-to-cart features: 1m-1h sliding windows. Medium for sell-through and look-to-book: 7d / 30d / 90d. Long for elasticity / seasonal baselines: 180d-2y, but those baselines typically live in the warehouse (not beava) and are refreshed into beava as scalar per-SKU baselines. Per-event_id ticketing state TTLs at event_date + 1d. Per-(SKU, store) state TTLs after 90 d of zero activity. Per-competitor-anchor state TTLs at the configured scrape staleness threshold (24h-7d). Per-(origin, dest, dep_date) state evicts on dep_date+1.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20-100+ features per pricing decision. Retail RM: 30-80 (own demand counters across windows + sell-through + competitor anchors across competitor set + seasonal baselines + promo flags). Surge: 10-30 (own-cell supply, demand, neighbouring-cell supply, recent-multiplier history). Airline: 50-150 (origin-dest-date-class × multiple windows + competitor anchors + days-to-departure + class-mix). Hotel: 30-80. Ticketing: 20-60. All strongly favour beava's batch_get path.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe is the baseline (a node losing its rolling 24h sell-through window for a Black Friday recovery period is hours of degraded pricing accuracy and millions in revenue impact on a mid-sized retailer). Regulator-grade durability is required for EU Omnibus 'reference-price' / 'lowest price in last 30 days' disclosure and for any future Digital Fairness Act personalised-pricing audit trail — but the regulator-grade artifact is the warehouse, not in-memory counters. Beava's WAL + snapshot story covers the live-counter durability tier; the regulator-grade tier is separate.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for single-binary regional / edge deployments next to the pricing service: a per-region retail RGM beava (US-East, EU, APAC), a per-city ride-hailing surge beava, a per-data-center airline-shop beava, a per-region hotel-RM SaaS beava, a per-venue ticketing beava. Hard ceilings: beava v0 has no in-process sharding (global Amazon / Booking / Uber aggregate exceeds a single box), no native multi-tenancy (problematic for hotel-RM SaaS vendors hosting thousands of properties on shared infra), refuse-on-network-FS forces local-disk WAL planning, no built-in TLS/auth disqualifies any internet-exposed deployment, and no multi-region active-active in v0.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Pricing / Revenue Growth Management (RGM) / Revenue Management / Pricing Science engineering teams at (a) e-comm and omnichannel retailers (Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, AO, Costco, Tesco, Carrefour, Otto, MediaMarkt, Currys, Wayfair, Wayflyer, Shein, Temu, Zalando, Boohoo, ASOS, Academy Sports + Outdoors), (b) ride-hailing and food-delivery (Uber, Lyft, Grab, FreeNow, Bolt, Didi, DoorDash, Instacart, Deliveroo, Just Eat, Postmates, Grubhub, Uber Eats), (c) airlines and OTAs (Delta, United, American, Lufthansa, IAG, Air France-KLM, Southwest, Ryanair, Qantas, Singapore, Emirates; Booking, Expedia, Trip.com, Skyscanner, Hopper), (d) hotels and short-term rentals (Marriott, Hilton, IHG, Accor, Hyatt; Airbnb, Vrbo, Vacasa, Sonder), (e) ticketing (Ticketmaster, Live Nation, AXS, SeatGeek, StubHub, Vivid Seats, Eventbrite), (f) marketplaces with seller-repricing (Amazon 3P sellers, eBay sellers, Walmart Marketplace sellers using Wiser / Sniffie-Pricen / Repricer.com / Aura), (g) energy utilities and demand-response operators (ComEd, NYISO, OhmConnect, Octopus Energy, GridBeyond), and (h) the pricing-software vendors themselves who would embed beava as the live-feature backend (Pricefx, PROS, Sniffie/Pricen, Competera, Wiser, RevenueAnalytics, Pricer24, Symson, Intelligence Node, PriceLabs, Beyond Pricing, IDeaS, Duetto, Atomize, Fetcherr, Flyr). The buyer is RGM Eng / Pricing Platform / Revenue Science — distinct from the data-science team that owns the models and the merchandising team that owns the rules.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: The directly-addressable price-optimization-software market is sized by Mordor Intelligence at USD 1.68B (2025) → USD 1.95B (2026) → USD 4.17B (2031), 16.06 % CAGR, North America 36.6 % share, APAC fastest at 16.9 % CAGR. The broader pricing-software / revenue-management / pricing-decision software TAM is roughly USD 5-10B in 2026 across price optimization, RM, CPQ, and competitor-price-intelligence. Vendor scale signals: Pricefx, PROS (publicly traded on NYSE), Vendavo, Zilliant, Revionics (acquired by Aptos), Blue Yonder, SAP CPM are the enterprise players; Sniffie/Pricen, Competera, Intelligence Node, Wiser, Pricer24, Skuuudle, 42Signals, Priceva, Pricefy are mid-market; Tecton publicly cites DoorDash as a flagship dynamic-pricing buyer; Hopsworks lists dynamic-pricing as a top use case; Wiser monitors '10B+ products and 200M+ prices daily'. Adoption signal: ~30 % of large European retailers reportedly use dynamic pricing (mostly online); McKinsey cites up to 5 % sales lift when real-time engines replace static tags; AO reports a 30 % conversion lift from real-time competitor + inventory features. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) EU regulation tightening: the Omnibus Directive (Art. 6a, in force since May 2022) requires 'lowest price in last 30 days' disclosure for any discount / sale price, which forces retailers to maintain and serve a rolling 30-day price-history feature with audit-grade durability. The proposed Digital Fairness Act (Q4 2026 legislative proposal) targets 'unfair personalised pricing that exploits consumer vulnerabilities,' which will likely force per-user disclosure and challenge feature provenance. The Consumer Rights Directive already requires disclosing when a price is personalised. 2) Inflation and margin compression continue to push retailers toward AI repricing (Walmart's AI-pricing patent filings reported in 2026; Amazon's well-known ~2.5M-price-changes-per-day cadence). 3) Surge-pricing political pressure: the US Senate's 2026 Ticketmaster Pricemaster / Platinum-pricing report; multiple state-level surge-pricing investigations of ride-hailing and food-delivery; Norway's hotel-pricing investigations. 4) Vendor consolidation and stack modernization: Tecton, Hopsworks, Chalk, Fennel, and Databricks are actively marketing dynamic-pricing as a feature-store use case, displacing in-house Redis+Lua+Flink stacks (DoorDash's published migration from SQS+Kinesis to Kafka+Flink, Lyft's Kafka-based pricing pipeline). 5) Energy-grid real-time pricing expansion under DOE / ISO programs (NYISO, ComEd Hourly Pricing). 6) Continuous-pricing modernization in airlines (PROS Real-Time Dynamic Pricing, Fetcherr's class-free continuous pricing, IATA NDC / Offers & Orders) — every legacy carrier is at some stage of replacing class-based RBD pricing with continuous-price ML.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: EU Omnibus Directive Art. 6a — 'reference price = lowest price in last 30 days' disclosure on all discount announcements (in force May 2022). EU Consumer Rights Directive Art. 6(1)(ea) — personalisation disclosure (in force May 2022). Proposed EU Digital Fairness Act (DFA) — Q4 2026 legislative proposal, targets unfair personalised pricing and price-discrimination practices; will likely require per-decision audit trail. GDPR / CCPA on user_id / session_id / device_fp used as pricing features (right-to-erasure must cascade through derived aggregates). PCI-DSS where pricing is integrated with checkout. US INFORM Consumers Act (high-volume marketplace seller verification) where the buyer is a marketplace repricer. Airline pricing is bound by DOT 14 CFR Part 399 truth-in-advertising rules (full-fare disclosure including ancillaries). Surge pricing in many US states is bound by disclosure / cap rules (NYC, Chicago, Massachusetts ride-hailing rules). State-level energy-pricing tariffs are filed and capped. SOC 2 Type II is table stakes for any enterprise pricing-vendor procurement. For ticketing, several US states cap dynamic-pricing increments above face value (anti-scalping). For groceries / pharma / fuel, anti-price-gouging statutes apply during declared emergencies (most US states).
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 2-5 days to a working per-SKU view-velocity + 30-day sell-through + competitor-anchor demo on beava, since @bv.event + @bv.table primitives map directly to the published feature definitions (view-to-cart-rate, sell-through, look-to-book, supply/demand ratio). A realistic 30-80-feature production pilot at a mid-sized retailer or per-city ride-hailing buyer is a 3-8 week effort once TLS, auth, multi-tenancy, and Omnibus-compatible price-history retention are added (the v0 gaps below). The natural one-page README example for this vertical is a 'flash-sale repricer' showing per-SKU view-velocity / atc-rate / sell-through + competitor anchor across a 15-min sliding window, which complements the existing python/beava/demos/ecommerce buyer-side demo.

competition.incumbents: Generic real-time stack dominated by Redis (counters + Lua + Redis Stack with Bloom / CMS / Top-K) for hot demand counters and surge multipliers, often in front of Kafka + Flink / Spark Streaming for the heavy windowing. DoorDash's Iguazu is Kafka + Flink at hundreds-of-billions of events/day. Lyft runs Kafka + Flink keyed by H3 for surge. Uber's surge stack is Kafka + geo-sharded services with H3. Airbnb's dynamic-pricing pipeline is Kafka + Spark + Cassandra + S3. Online feature-store competitors: Tecton (publicly names dynamic pricing as a top use case; DoorDash flagship; sub-10 ms p99, 100k+ QPS, sub-1 s freshness on Redis + DynamoDB + proprietary caching), Hopsworks (RonDB online store, 250k+ ops/sec, 7.5 ms p99, Clicklease micro-lease case study), Chalk (Kafka streaming + batch sources, defined feature DSL), Feast (open-source, batch + online), Fennel (Rust-native streaming feature store positioning itself directly against Tecton on freshness), Databricks Feature Store. Adjacent: Materialize / RisingWave / ksqlDB for SQL-on-streams demand pipelines (Riskified runs ksqlDB + Flink); ScyllaDB / Aerospike / DynamoDB as the online KV for low-latency feature reads. Reinforcement-learning / contextual-bandit servers like Vowpal Wabbit, RLlib, and Outerbounds Metaflow.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: End-to-end pricing-decision SaaS (would embed beava as the feature backend or compete head-on at the decision layer): Retail / e-comm RGM and competitor monitoring — Pricefx, PROS (also airline), Vendavo, Zilliant, Revionics (Aptos), Blue Yonder, SAP CPM, Symson, Intelligence Node, Sniffie/Pricen, Competera, Wiser, Pricer24, Skuuudle, 42Signals, Prisync, Priceva, Pricefy, Repricer.com (marketplace seller), Aura (Amazon FBA), Eva.com (Amazon), Bonsai. Hotel revenue management — IDeaS (SAS), Duetto, Atomize, RoomPriceGenie, PriceLabs, Beyond Pricing, Wheelhouse, Hospitable, Hostfully, BeyondPricing. Airline RM and continuous pricing — PROS, Fetcherr, Flyr, Sabre RMS, Amadeus RM, IBS Software. Ride-hailing and food-delivery dynamic pricing — entirely in-house at Uber, Lyft, Bolt, Grab, DoorDash, Instacart, Deliveroo. Ticketing dynamic pricing — Ticketmaster Pricemaster / Live Nation in-house, AXS, SeatGeek pricing, StubHub Repricer. Energy / grid — GridBeyond, EnergyHub, Voltus, AutoGrid, Octopus Kraken, Bidgely. Marketplace seller repricing — Repricer.com, Aura, Eva, BQool, ChannelMAX, Seller Snap, Informed.co (formerly Appeagle). Beava more naturally sits underneath one of these vendors or an in-house pricing platform than replaces them end-to-end — it is the feature-store layer, not the elasticity/RL scorer or the merchandiser UI.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Redis cluster — fits per-region / per-city / per-venue sidecar topologies that smaller pricing vendors (PriceLabs, Beyond, Repricer.com, Aura, Symson) and many in-house single-region teams actually deploy. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives natively cover view-velocity / sell-through / look-to-book / supply-demand-ratio / basket-affinity / competitor-anchor features, no Lua / Flink-SQL needed. 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get fits the tens-of-ms inline pricing budget with material headroom; in published benchmarks beava is the same order of magnitude faster than Tecton's stated sub-10 ms p99 and Hopsworks' 7.5 ms p99. 4) Native composite-key (pair / triple) aggregations — (SKU, H3), (SKU, competitor_id), (origin, dest, dep_date), (hotel_id, check_in_date), (anchor_sku, candidate_sku), (h3_cell, time_bucket) — which Redis requires hand-rolled hash-of-hash schemes for and which are exactly the keying shape pricing buyers want. 5) Apache-2.0, no open-core — attractive to mid-market pricing vendors (Sniffie/Pricen, Competera, Wiser, Pricer24, PriceLabs, Beyond, Symson) who want to embed it rather than pay Tecton, and to large in-house teams (Walmart, Target, Booking, Uber, DoorDash, Ticketmaster) who do not want vendor lock-in on a margin-critical control plane. 6) Distance primitive cleanly expresses 'own_price − median_competitor_price' and 'observed_competitor_price − last_observed' (competitor-move-detection) and 'days-to-departure' / 'days-to-event' anchors. 7) Push-on-event ingestion matches how scrapers (Wiser, Sniffie, 42Signals), pricing-event services, and clickstream collectors already emit events — no broker hop. 8) Sliding windows over 30 d align exactly with EU Omnibus 'lowest price in last 30 days' — a rare alignment between a generic feature store and a regulator-enforced metric.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth in v0 on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 — disqualifying for any production pricing deployment; SOC 2 / PCI / Omnibus / DFA audit programs all require authenticated access to revenue-critical infrastructure. 2) No in-process sharding — global Amazon / Walmart / global Uber / global Booking / global Airbnb pricing aggregates exceed a single box; the single-tenant ceiling is roughly ~684k EPS and ~100-150 GB hot state. 3) Refuse-on-network-FS plus in-memory-only means buyers must plan local-disk WAL and bound cold-start replay time. 4) No triggers / 'fire when (sku).sell_through_rate_30d crosses 80 % then auto-reorder' or 'when (h3_cell).sd_ratio crosses 1.5x then publish surge multiplier' — pricing is fundamentally event-driven (auto-markdown, auto-reorder, auto-surge, auto-promo), today that has to be polled or done in the scorer. 5) No multi-tenancy primitives — hotel-RM SaaS (PriceLabs, Beyond, IDeaS, Duetto) hosting thousands of properties on shared infrastructure need per-property namespaces, quotas, and per-tenant rate-limit accounting. 6) No secondary indexes / no 'list all SKUs with sell_through_30d < 20 %' or 'top-K H3 cells by sd_ratio in last 5 min' analyst query — kills the merchant / dispatcher / RM-analyst surface. 7) No native ML-feature-versioning / training-serving-skew toolchain that Tecton, Hopsworks, Chalk, Feast, and Fennel all ship — a real gap for data-science buyers who train pricing elasticity / RL models offline and serve them online. 8) No native time-travel or point-in-time backfill — required by elasticity / contextual-bandit training pipelines to avoid future leakage. 9) No native price-history audit-log primitive (regulator-grade Omnibus tier lives in a warehouse, not beava). 10) No native cross-region / multi-region active-active for global pricing buyers. 11) No native Kafka / Kinesis / Flink integration — every existing pricing buyer's source-of-events stack assumes a broker; documenting the push-from-Kafka-consumer / push-from-Flink-sink pattern is critical.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: e-commerce front-end (HTTP push for views / searches / add-to-carts directly or via segment-style collector; alternative is a Kafka consumer pushing into beava), order/checkout service, inventory / ERP webhook (HTTP), price-change service (own + promo), competitor-scrape workers (HTTP push of (competitor_id, sku, observed_price, observed_availability, scrape_age)) from Wiser / Sniffie / Pricer24 / 42Signals / Priceva / in-house scrapers, marketplace API (Amazon SP-API, Walmart Connect, eBay Trading, Shopify, Mirakl, Adobe Commerce), driver / courier telemetry (TCP+msgpack for high-volume position updates), shopping engine / GDS feed (Amadeus, Sabre, Travelport for airlines), PMS / channel manager (SiteMinder, Cloudbeds, Mews, Apaleo for hotels), grid telemetry (OSIsoft PI, AVEVA, ISO market data for energy), ticketing / box-office system (Ticketmaster TM1, AXS, SeatGeek). Consumers: pricing rules engines (Drools, FEEL, Pricefx's own DSL, Pricer24's rule engine, in-house Lua / Python), ML scorers (XGBoost / LightGBM for retail elasticity, contextual bandits / RLlib / Vowpal Wabbit for surge / continuous, transformer-based demand forecasters, PROS / Fetcherr / Flyr scorers for airline), and the inline price-render in PDP / quote / fare / room-rate / fare-quote / surge-multiplier paths. The pricing rules engine + the ML scorer + the rendering surface all read from the same batch_get on beava.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. Pricing is uniquely a hybrid of rules and ML. Hard rules (regulatory caps, anti-gouging floors, brand-pricing-policy MAP, EU Omnibus reference-price clamps, currency-cents rounding, end-in-99 psychological floors, daily price-change-velocity caps) are deterministic and live in a rules engine. ML / RL scorers (elasticity GLM, XGBoost, LightGBM, contextual bandits, deep-RL like Fetcherr's, transformer demand forecasters) compute the candidate price. Beava as a pure feature backend stays decoupled — both the rules engine and the ML scorer read from the same batch_get path, and the rules engine consumes the same per-SKU sell-through / view-velocity / competitor-anchor features as the model.

adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Mixed but generally passive load with adversarial sub-paths. The dominant load is passive: views, searches, driver-positions, availability-queries, meter-reads. Adversarial sub-paths exist: (1) bots that pump view counters to manipulate trending-product surfacing or to scrape competitor prices, (2) coordinated buying bursts on ticketing (the broker-bot economy), (3) reinforcement-learning-style adversarial pricing by competitors who themselves run repricers and can be probed, (4) consumer click-farm gaming for dynamic-discount eligibility. Feature drift is moderate — seasonal and trend-driven rather than fraudster-driven — which argues for periodic retraining but does not require the daily / weekly feature-add cadence that fraud (item 1a) and account-abuse (item 2) impose. Stability / cost optimization matters more than maximum-adversarial robustness.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) The price-optimization scorer / RL agent / elasticity estimator itself — that is the proprietary IP of Pricefx, PROS, Sniffie, Competera, Fetcherr, Flyr, Tecton-customers' XGBoost / RL models. Beava is the feature backend, not the model server. 2) Long historical lookback for elasticity training, baselining, and Omnibus 30-day reference-price audit reports — beava is in-memory; that belongs in Parquet / a lakehouse. The 30-day Omnibus window can be served from beava live, but the audit-grade artifact is the warehouse. 3) Cross-tenant aggregated benchmarks ('your competitive set's median sell-through') — that is the network effect of Wiser, Competera, Intelligence Node, PriceLabs market-data; beava is single-tenant by design. 4) Forecasting itself (LSTM / Prophet / DeepAR / temporal-fusion-transformers) — beava provides the historical aggregates the forecaster consumes. 5) The competitor-scraping infrastructure — that is the IP of Wiser, Sniffie, Bright Data, Oxylabs, Apify. Beava ingests the scrape output as events. 6) Acting as the merchant UI, the price-rule editor, the markdown-cadence planner, the campaign manager, or the Omnibus audit-export tool — beava is the feature backend. 7) Sub-tariff energy market settlement (FERC- / ISO-grade financial ledger) — beava counters are not the source of truth for money. 8) Multi-region active-active in v0. 9) GDS / NDC offer construction — beava feeds the RM scorer that informs the offer, but does not assemble offer instances or persist them as legal contracts. 10) Cross-channel personalized-pricing audit trail under future DFA — requires regulator-grade durability and per-user provenance that beava v0 does not ship.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for dynamic pricing, in priority order: 1) TLS termination and mutual TLS on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 plus an auth model (token, mTLS, or both) on the push and admin surfaces — without this, no SOC 2 / PCI-adjacent / Omnibus-compliant retailer, hotel-RM SaaS, airline, or marketplace can deploy externally. This is the same blocker that limits items 1a / 9 / 10 — the single most important gap. 2) Triggers / 'fire callback when (sku).sell_through_30d crosses 80 % then call /reorder' or 'when (h3_cell).sd_ratio crosses 1.5x then publish surge multiplier' — pricing is fundamentally event-driven, polling 30-100 features per tick to threshold them is wasteful on the 5-min repricing path and the 30-60 s surge path. 3) First-class composite-key (pair / triple) aggregations — (sku, h3), (sku, competitor_id), (sku, store_id), (origin, dest, dep_date, fare_class), (hotel_id, check_in_date, room_type), (anchor_sku, candidate_sku), (event_id, section), (grid_cell, tariff_id) — these are the load-bearing keying shapes and need ergonomic @bv.table syntax. 4) HLL / Bloom / CMS / Top-K as first-class aggregations to bound cardinality on (sku, h3), (sku, competitor_id), and trending-SKU views; if present in the 50+ primitives, document them with worked examples ('top-K H3 cells by sd_ratio in last 5 min', 'top-K SKUs by view-velocity in last 1 h'). 5) In-process or sidecar sharding by key prefix (sku, h3, origin-dest) for Amazon-3P / global-Uber / global-Booking scale. 6) Per-key TTL / sliding-window eviction aligned with pricing windows (1m / 5m / 1h / 24h / 30d) so (sku, h3) / (sku, competitor) / (origin, dest, dep_date) cardinality stays bounded. 7) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting for vendors serving many merchants / properties (PriceLabs, Beyond, IDeaS, Duetto, Sniffie/Pricen, Competera, Wiser, Pricer24, Repricer.com, Aura). 8) Time-travel / point-in-time backfill for elasticity-model training and contextual-bandit replay — required to avoid future leakage; this is the table-stakes online/offline-consistency feature Tecton, Hopsworks, Chalk, Feast, and Fennel all advertise. 9) Streaming admin / debug surface + secondary indexes so RM analysts can run 'top-K SKUs by 30d_sell_through < 20 %' or 'top-K H3 cells by sd_ratio' without materializing the whole keyspace. 10) PII-handling story: user_id / session_id / device_fp hashing at rest, configurable per-namespace retention, right-to-erasure that cascades through derived aggregates (GDPR, DFA). 11) Documented Kafka / Kinesis / Flink ingest pattern (push-from-Kafka-consumer, push-from-Flink-sink) — every existing pricing buyer's source stack assumes a broker; beava-native push is unfamiliar. 12) Cold-start strategy: WAL replay on tens of GB of hot SKU / (SKU, h3) / (SKU, competitor) state must be benchmarked and bounded. 13) Reference architecture for the Omnibus 30-day-reference-price feature with regulator-grade durability backed by a warehouse and live serving from beava. 14) Native price-history-audit-log primitive for future DFA personalised-pricing audit. 15) Native demand-response / load-curve primitive (rolling kWh per grid cell, peak-to-average ratio, time-of-use bucket counters) for energy buyers. 16) Documented hooks for cross-region replication once a buyer exceeds single-region.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — strongly. Dynamic pricing genuinely needs an event-driven trigger primitive: 'when (sku).sell_through_30d crosses 80 % then call /reorder API', 'when (sku).sell_through_30d falls below 20 % then call /markdown API', 'when (h3_cell).sd_ratio_5m crosses 1.5x then publish surge multiplier to /surge', 'when (sku).view_velocity_15m crosses N × baseline then re-quote', 'when (origin, dest, dep_date).bookings_24h > target then move fare-class boundary', 'when (event_id, section).sales_velocity_1h > target then bump tier'. Polling 30-100 features per pricing tick is workable on the inline read path because the read is already happening, but is wasteful and high-latency on the asynchronous repricing-tick / surge-publish / markdown / reorder / fare-class-rebucket path. This is one of the two most-cited gaps for the domain along with TLS + auth.
